# gopher-tool

## Project overview

Command-line tool that tidies Go module files. It runs locally and in CI.

Core features:
- Sort require blocks

## Language policy

- Code, comments, docs and commit messages: English.
- Replies to the user: English.

## Tech stack

Uses: Go, golangci-lint.

## Commands

- Build: `go build ./...`
- Test: `go test ./...`
- Lint: `golangci-lint run`

## Code style

- Format code with gofmt. Return errors instead of panicking, and wrap them with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)`. Why: gofmt ends style debates, and wrapped errors keep the context needed to debug a failure.
- Run `golangci-lint run` before finishing a change and fix every finding. Suppress a finding only with a `//nolint` that names the linter and gives a reason, as in `//nolint:gosec // path is a constant`. Why: A suppression that names its linter and reason can be reviewed, while a bare one hides future problems.
- App locale: en.

## Agent workflow

- The user is learning Go. The first time you use a construct or idiom, explain it in one or two sentences. Work in small steps instead of writing whole modules at once. For simple parts, describe what to write and let the user write it, then review their code. Why: The user wants to understand the code, not just receive it.
- For any change beyond one file, propose a short plan with the files to touch and the approach, and wait for approval before writing code. Why: Correcting a plan costs one message, while correcting finished code costs a rewrite.
- Never edit the agent instruction files or `cyanotype.yaml` yourself. When you learn a convention, or are corrected twice on the same point, propose a rule with its reason for the user to approve. Why: The instruction files are generated from `cyanotype.yaml`, so direct edits are lost and unreviewed rules creep in.

## Code review

- Before asking for review, reread the diff and remove debug output. Why: Reviewers should spend their time on design, not leftovers.

## Other rules

- Keep the changelog in `CHANGELOG.md`. Add an entry for every user-visible change. Why: Users read the changelog, not the git log.

## Safety rules

- Keep secrets in `.env`, which stays in `.gitignore`; never hardcode or commit them, and do not read `.env` files. When you add a variable, add its name with a placeholder value to `.env.example`. Why: A committed secret stays in git history and has to be rotated.

## Domain notes

Module paths are case-sensitive.

Never touch vendor/.

- Keep the CLI output under 80 columns. Why: Users run it in narrow CI logs.

## Further reading

- Before adding a feature, read docs/PRODUCT.md.
